title: ongawa (formerly virtuosos)
label: ongawa
summary: Former CTO at Virtuosos, the rhythm-game company that became Ongawa.

sections.heading: my role
paragraphs: I served as CTO at Virtuosos, which became Ongawa. I worked with programmers, artists, and musicians to build the rhythm game in Unity. The game combined timed musical input with characters, environments, and visual-novel storytelling.

sections.heading: rhythm gameplay
paragraphs: Our Conductor system tracks song position using Unity’s audio clock and schedules musical sections ahead of time. Notes approach the player through linear interpolation and bounce away with cosine interpolation after a successful hit.

image.alt: Virtuosos rhythm gameplay with note tracks and a score display
image.caption: Note tracks, score, and timing feedback in an early Virtuosos build.

sections.heading: input and calibration
paragraphs: We moved input handling into Action Maps to support different controllers. A calibration screen measures the average timing offset of a player’s ten most recent presses so they can adjust for their screen and speakers.

sections.heading: ongawa
paragraphs: Ongawa describes the game as a mix of rhythm gameplay and role-playing, with a focus on music, creativity, and discovering musical talent. These images show the earlier Virtuosos build.

image.alt: Virtuosos rhythm game cover artwork
image.caption: Cover artwork from the early Virtuosos project.

title: gunfight
label: gunfight
summary: My first online multiplayer game: a top-down shooter.

sections.heading: my role
paragraphs: I led the design and project management and programmed the game. Lucas Li created the sprite artwork and implemented post-processing. I used a 1970s-inspired vector palette.

image.alt: Four graphic studies using the earth-tone Gunfight palette
image.caption: The 1970s-inspired color palette used in Gunfight.

sections.heading: camera and weapons
paragraphs: The camera follows a point between the player and the mouse, with interpolation to smooth its movement. Shooting uses a 2D raycast and layered particles for visual feedback. Thrown weapons use momentum and angular velocity.

sections.heading: multiplayer
paragraphs: I used Steamworks and Mirror for Steam lobbies and client/server communication. In the first ten weeks, I completed a free-for-all mode with rounds, multiple weapons, shooting mechanics, and online multiplayer. The planned team mode was not part of that version.

image.alt: Gunfight’s top-down arena after post-processing
image.caption: Gunfight’s arena, with Lucas Li’s sprites and post-processing.

title: experience
label: experience
summary: A first-person game built in C++ and OpenGL.

sections.heading: the game
paragraphs: I made Experience with Lucas Li and Alex Hartford in ten weeks. Players walk, observe, read notes, and talk with animals across three environments. Each represents a stage of learning: a forest at the beginning, a desert in the difficult middle, and a quiet street at the end.

sections.heading: engine
paragraphs: We built the game in C++ and OpenGL, using libraries for windows, mesh loading, and audio. The renderer includes instancing, shadow mapping, bloom, Gaussian blur, and view frustum culling.

image.alt: A bright sunset in Experience with bloom and blur applied
image.caption: Bloom and Gaussian blur soften bright areas.

sections.heading: level editor
paragraphs: We built a level editor for objects, lighting, shadows, audio, and particles. It saves levels in an ASCII format that the game can load.

image.alt: The Experience level editor showing scene objects and an editing panel
image.caption: Object placement and scene settings in the level editor.

image.alt: An environment from the first-person game Experience

title: procedural animation
label: motion
summary: Spider movement generated in real time with inverse kinematics.

sections.heading: the project
paragraphs: For my computer animation final project at Cal Poly, I taught myself procedural animation in C++ and OpenGL. Moving a spider’s body makes its legs adjust and step.

sections.heading: leg positions
paragraphs: I implemented FABRIK, an inverse kinematics algorithm, to position each leg’s joints around a target. When the body moves too far from a leg’s target, that leg takes a new step.

image.alt: A diagram of a joint chain reaching toward a target through FABRIK passes
image.caption: Backward and forward passes reposition a joint chain while preserving segment lengths.

sections.heading: stepping
paragraphs: I added a target halfway through each step and above the ground so the feet lift instead of sliding. Each leg interpolates through that point before landing. A simple AI moves and rotates the bodies so the spiders wander.

image.alt: Procedural spiders walking across a yellow ground plane
image.caption: Leg targets and stepping logic generate the walk as the bodies move.

image.alt: Procedural spiders with articulated legs

title: timing calibration
label: timing
summary: Adjusting rhythm-game timing for different screens and speakers.

sections.heading: input delay
paragraphs: Different screens and speakers introduce different delays. We built a calibration interface on Virtuosos’s start screen so players could adjust the offset while listening to the music.

sections.heading: measuring the offset
paragraphs: Each press is measured against the beat using Unity’s audio engine. The screen shows the average offset of the ten most recent presses, which players use to adjust the alignment of sound and visual cues.

image.alt: The Virtuosos calibration screen with timing markers and an input prompt
image.caption: Input timing calibration against the background beat.

title: audio clock
label: audio clock
summary: Using Unity’s audio timeline to synchronize rhythm gameplay.

sections.heading: song position
paragraphs: Our Conductor class in Virtuosos tracks the song’s position, beats, and bars. It uses Unity’s audio clock rather than the game clock, so gameplay follows the same timeline as the music.

sections.heading: scheduled playback
paragraphs: The system schedules upcoming background music and instrumental sections ahead of time. Song position also determines where notes appear on their tracks and when the player should hit them.

image.alt: The Virtuosos note track with annotated spawner and trigger positions
image.caption: Notes travel from the spawner toward the player’s trigger using song position.

title: keyboard & controller input
label: inputs
summary: Using Unity Action Maps for keyboard and controller bindings.

sections.heading: direct button checks
paragraphs: Our early Virtuosos code checked individual keyboard and controller buttons directly. Each new input layout required more checks in the gameplay code.

sections.heading: action maps
paragraphs: We moved to Unity Action Maps. Gameplay refers to an input action, and its bindings define the keys or buttons that trigger it. This keeps the bindings in one place and makes controller support easier to change.

image.alt: Unity input actions with keyboard and controller bindings for Virtuosos
image.caption: Input actions collect keyboard and controller bindings in one map.

title: steam lobbies
label: lobbies

sections.heading: lobby system
paragraphs: Gunfight was my first online game. I used Steamworks and Mirror to build a lobby system that players could join through Steam. It also displayed their Steam usernames and profile pictures.

sections.heading: gameplay synchronization
paragraphs: I used Commands and client RPCs to synchronize movement, firing, weapon spawning, and hit detection between the server and players.

title: camera movement
label: camera
summary: A camera that follows the player and mouse position in Gunfight.

sections.heading: player and mouse position
paragraphs: I programmed Gunfight’s top-down camera to track the midpoint between the player and the mouse.

sections.heading: smoothing
paragraphs: The midpoint interpolates within a defined radius to smooth the camera’s movement. It was one of the first systems I worked on.

title: weapon throws
label: momentum
summary: Using momentum and angular velocity to animate thrown weapons.

sections.heading: throwing
paragraphs: In Gunfight, I applied momentum and angular velocity to thrown weapons to move and rotate them.

sections.heading: shooting
paragraphs: Firing uses layered particle systems to show a bullet’s movement. Throwing uses the movement of the weapon itself.

title: inverse kinematics
label: ik
summary: The FABRIK solver used for my procedural spider legs.

sections.heading: backward pass
paragraphs: I used FABRIK to calculate the joint positions of each spider leg. The solver works backward from the target, repositioning joints while preserving each segment’s length.

sections.heading: forward pass
paragraphs: A forward pass restores the leg’s starting point and adjusts the remaining joints. Repeating the passes moves the end toward its target. I represented each leg as an array of points in C++; the animation system chooses a target, and the solver calculates the joint positions.

image.alt: A development view of procedural spider legs and target points
image.caption: A development view of the leg chains and their moving target points.

paragraphs: We built a level editor alongside the game engine for Experience. It lets us edit objects, lighting, shadows, audio, particles, and distance fog.

sections.heading: level files
paragraphs: The editor saves levels in an ASCII format that the game can load. We used it to build the forest, desert, and street environments.
